title: IIT Bombay Director Signs 18-Point Charter, Apologises Amid Protests Over Student's Death
excerpt: After a three-day sit-in over Sahil Wakode's death, Director Shireesh Kedare agreed to an independent probe and institutional reforms; the institute denied rumors of his resignation.
body:
• IIT Bombay Director Prof. Shireesh Kedare signed an 18-point student charter late Sunday after a three-day sit-in, agreeing to take forward demands for an independent probe into the death of second-year student Sahil Wakode and sweeping institutional reforms.
  • The charter demands an independent investigation with an interim report by Sept. 30, action against those found responsible, and changes to mental-health support, faculty conduct rules and disciplinary processes.
  • Students demanded the immediate suspension of Prof. Suryanarayana Doolla, the invigilator who reported Wakode for allegedly using a phone during a mid-semester exam; the director said due process would be followed, though one outlet reports Doolla has been suspended.
  • The institute apologized Monday for its earlier statement on Wakode's death and denied social-media rumors that the director had resigned; an FIR naming Doolla and other officials is now with the Mumbai Crime Branch.

The standoff at the Indian Institute of Technology Bombay entered a new phase late Sunday after Director Prof. Shireesh Kedare signed an 18-point charter of demands submitted by protesting students, ending a three-day sit-in near the campus main gate over the death of second-year BTech student Sahil Wakode.

Kedare signed the document after nearly three hours of discussions with student representatives on Sunday, Sept. 20, according to India Today and multiple outlets. The charter commits the administration to take forward the protesters' demands — though an institute official later clarified that signing did not amount to an immediate decision on each individual demand, and that due process would be followed.

What the charter demands

The 18-point document centers on an independent investigation into the circumstances of Wakode's death, with students demanding an interim report by Sept. 30 and a final report by Oct. 15, along with action against those found responsible. Beyond the investigation, the charter proposes broad institutional reforms: an open house with the director, the Dean of Student Affairs and senior officials; an apology over what protesters described as the public defamation of Wakode; a code of conduct for professors; sensitization of faculty and staff on mental health; strengthened in-person counseling services; and a revision of the Disciplinary Action Committee process.

"We categorically state that the related news is false," the institute posted on X on Sept."

Wakode, a student in the Department of Energy Science and Engineering, was found dead in his hostel room on the Powai campus on Sept. 18. He had allegedly been caught with a mobile phone during a mid-semester examination earlier that day and accused of uploading the question paper to ChatGPT to obtain answers. The institute has maintained that no disciplinary action had been initiated against him before his death.

The professor at the center of the protests

One of the most contentious demands concerns Prof. Suryanarayana Doolla, who was invigilating the examination and reported Wakode for possessing the phone. Students demanded Doolla's immediate suspension. When the issue was raised during Sunday's meeting, Kedare was heard saying the institute would "follow the process," and an official later emphasized that the matter would be handled according to due procedure.

Doolla has also been named in a police FIR registered on Sept. 19 on a complaint by Wakode's parents, along with other institute officials, on charges of abetment of suicide under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita. Provisions of the SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act were invoked following the family's allegations of caste-based harassment — allegations that have not been established and remain under investigation. The probe has since been transferred to the Mumbai Crime Branch. On Monday, LatestLY reported that Doolla has been suspended; the institute has not issued an official confirmation of that step.

Apology and resignation rumors

In a fresh statement Monday, IIT Bombay apologized for details in its earlier communication about Wakode's death, saying it was inappropriate to describe or characterize events preceding his death before those details had been established through the investigative process. The institute stressed that conclusions about what happened should not have been presented before being established through the appropriate process.

The institute also moved to quash rumors circulating on social media — including videos claiming to show the director's resignation. "Director IIT Bombay has NOT resigned. We categorically state that the related news is false," the institute posted on X on Sept. 21. The Board of Governors held a special meeting on Monday, Sept. 21, and the details of the charter agreement are expected to be formally discussed with students at an open house.

Why it matters beyond Powai

The crisis at India's most prestigious engineering institute is being watched closely by the vast IIT alumni network abroad — tens of thousands of Indian-origin engineers and academics in the United States count an IIT as their alma mater, and many are parents weighing the same institutions for their children. The case has fused three issues the diaspora follows intensely: the pressures of India's high-stakes academic culture, allegations of caste discrimination on elite campuses, and the adequacy of mental-health support for students. How IIT Bombay handles the independent probe — and whether the charter's reforms materialize — will shape that conversation for years.

What to watch

The immediate tests are the Sept. 30 interim-report deadline, the promised open house on Monday, and the Crime Branch investigation. Longer term, the charter's demands — a faculty code of conduct, overhauled disciplinary processes, real counseling capacity — amount to a governance overhaul that few Indian institutions have attempted. Whether a signed charter becomes institutional change, or a document that quiets a protest, is the question now facing Kedare's administration.
